analysis.one_liner: Bars US foreign aid from funding the military detention and abuse of Palestinian children and funds monitoring and treatment programs.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or a vote in the House and died at the end of the 116th Congress in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Leahy law — the existing US statute that bars aid to foreign security forces that commit gross human-rights abuses — to specifically prohibit US funds from supporting the military detention, interrogation, abuse, or ill-treatment of children. It names practices that could not be funded, including torture, solitary confinement, administrative detention without charge, and coerced confessions, and it would create a $19 million-a-year State Department program funding NGOs to document abuses and provide rehabilitation to Palestinians detained as children. The bill cites findings that Israel detains roughly 500 to 700 Palestinian children a year in a military court system and that the US provides Israel more than $3.8 billion in annual military assistance [S3]. The bill did not change the total amount of aid; it would only have barred certain uses of it.
analysis.who_benefits: Palestinian children in the occupied West Bank would gain the most direct protection: US law would explicitly prohibit American funds from supporting their military detention, torture, solitary confinement, and detention without charge, and a new $19 million annual program would fund independent monitoring and trauma treatment for those affected [S2, S3]. American taxpayers would gain a clearer legal limit on how their military assistance dollars can be used, since the bill does not cut the more than $3.8 billion in annual aid but bars specific uses of it [S3].

how_it_helps.text: It amends the Leahy law so that no US foreign-assistance funds could support the military detention, interrogation, abuse, or ill-treatment of children in violation of international humanitarian law.

It specifically bars funding support for torture, physical violence, stress positions, hooding, sensory deprivation, solitary or incommunicado detention, administrative detention without charge, arbitrary detention, denial of parental or legal access during interrogation, and coerced confessions of children.

It authorizes at least $19 million a year for nongovernmental organizations to document abuses against detained Palestinian children and to provide treatment and rehabilitation to Palestinians 21 or younger who were detained as children.
It requires that documentation of abuses be made publicly available on the internet and in annual reports, with safeguards to protect victims and sources.

analysis.who_pays: No one loses money under the bill as written: it does not reduce the total US military assistance to Israel [S3]. The Israeli military would face new restrictions on practices it could carry out with US-supported funds, and would lose discretion over how detention of children is conducted and documented. Defenders of the alliance argued the conditions could strain US-Israel relations.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes conditions on US military assistance to Israel, which supporters of the alliance argue could strain a key security relationship and insert Congress into day-to-day conduct of an ally's legal system.

The $19 million annual monitoring and treatment program would be administered through nongovernmental organizations and depend on access to Israeli military detention facilities and records, which critics noted could be resisted, limiting how much the program could actually verify.

Because the restriction is tied to the Leahy law's framework, enforcement would depend on State Department determinations about how US-funded activities connect to specific detention practices — a mechanism that has historically been applied unevenly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but narrow: the bill would apply existing US human-rights law to a specific, well-documented practice and fund monitoring and treatment for affected children, at a modest $19 million per year against more than $3.8 billion in military assistance [S3]. The main drawbacks are practical: conditioning aid could strain a key alliance and be difficult to verify from Washington, and Israel would likely object to outside monitoring of its military courts. But the bill does not cut off aid overall, so the cost to the alliance is a condition on how funds are used, not an end to support.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Foreign Affairs Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 30, 2019 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs.
The House Foreign Affairs Committee never reported the bill, held no markup on it, and the full House never voted on it.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill expired without any action beyond the initial referral.
It attracted 26 cosponsors, all Democrats, out of 231 House Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held: US military assistance to Israel continued without any conditions tied to the treatment of Palestinian children, and no new human-rights monitoring program was created. The committee leadership that declined to act on the bill kept it off the agenda.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Supporters of the aid status quo

for.name: Rep. Betty McCollum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on April 30, 2019.

against.name: House Committee on Foreign Affairs leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after its referral, so it never advanced.

against.name: Pro-Israel lobbying organizations, including AIPAC
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill and lobbied against conditionality on US military aid to Israel; the bill drew no Republican cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: All 26 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republicans signed on, and the committee majority that declined to act was controlled by the same party as the sponsor — the bill had no Republican support at any stage [S4].

industries.industry: US defense contractors (foreign military financing recipients)
industries.note: The bill does not cut the more than $3.8 billion in annual US military assistance to Israel [S3]; it conditions how some funds can be used, leaving the overall flow of aid — which is largely spent on US-made weapons — intact even if enacted. As introduced and never voted on, the existing unconditional arrangement continued unchanged.

If enacted, the bill would create a new $19 million annual funding stream for NGOs doing monitoring and trauma treatment [S2, S3], a gain for that sector. Because the bill died, no such funding was created.
